title: Common Table Expressions & Recursion
summary: Naming subqueries for readability, then extending that same syntax to walk hierarchies and graphs that a plain join can't traverse.

slides.markdown:
A **Common Table Expression (CTE)** — the `WITH name AS (...)` block before a query — gives a subquery a name you can reference later, turning a nested mess into a readable sequence of steps. That alone makes CTEs worth knowing.

The bigger reason they matter in interviews: a **recursive** CTE can reference itself, which is the only standard-SQL way to walk a hierarchy of unknown depth — an org chart, a category tree, a friend-of-a-friend graph — without knowing in advance how many levels deep you'll go.

A CTE lets you name an intermediate result and reference it like a table for the rest of the query — you can chain several, each building on the last.

```sql
WITH high_value_orders AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
  HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000
),
repeat_customers AS (
  SELECT customer_id FROM high_value_orders
  WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 3)
)
SELECT * FROM repeat_customers;
```

The same logic nested as subqueries would be three levels of parentheses deep and hard to read top to bottom. A CTE reads like a sequence of named steps — closer to how you'd actually explain the logic out loud.

slides.sectionTitle: Recursive CTE: anchor plus recursive member
slides.markdown:
A recursive CTE has two parts joined by `UNION ALL`. The **anchor member** is a normal query that produces the starting rows. The **recursive member** references the CTE's own name and runs repeatedly, each time operating on the *previous* iteration's output, until it returns zero rows.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (
  SELECT employee_id, manager_id, 1 AS depth   -- anchor: top of the tree
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.employee_id, e.manager_id, oc.depth + 1  -- recursive member
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org_chart oc ON e.manager_id = oc.employee_id
)
SELECT * FROM org_chart;
```

The engine effectively loops: run the anchor once, then keep re-running the recursive member against only the newest batch of rows, accumulating results, until a pass produces nothing new.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking an org tree or a graph path
slides.markdown:
The same pattern walks any hierarchy without knowing its depth up front — an org chart, a bill-of-materials, a category tree, or the shortest path in a graph. Add a column that accumulates a path or distance as you go:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE reachable AS (
  SELECT to_city AS city, 1 AS hops, ARRAY[from_city, to_city] AS path
  FROM routes WHERE from_city = 'NYC'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT r.to_city, re.hops + 1, re.path || r.to_city
  FROM routes r
  JOIN reachable re ON r.from_city = re.city
  WHERE NOT r.to_city = ANY(re.path)  -- avoid revisiting a city
)
SELECT city, MIN(hops) FROM reachable GROUP BY city;
```

The `NOT r.to_city = ANY(re.path)` guard is doing double duty here — it prevents cycles in the graph *and* is what makes termination guaranteed, since each recursive step can only add cities not already visited.

Each recursive pass adds exactly one level of depth — the engine can't "skip ahead" to grandchildren before it has processed children, because the recursive member only sees the previous iteration's output as its input.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: missing termination means infinite recursion
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I wrote a `WITH RECURSIVE` query, so it'll just figure out when to stop."

**Why it's wrong:** the recursion only stops when a pass produces **zero new rows**. If your data has a cycle (employee A reports to B, B reports to A — a data-quality bug, but it happens) and you never filtered against a visited-path column, every iteration keeps producing rows forever. Most engines cap this with a `max_recursion` limit or statement timeout and the query eventually errors out, but not before consuming real resources.

**Correct model:** always design the recursive member so a strictly monotonic quantity — depth, a path array of visited nodes, a decreasing remaining budget — guarantees the row count trends to zero. For graph traversal specifically, guard against revisiting a node explicitly (`WHERE NOT x = ANY(path)`), don't assume the source data has no cycles.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: CTE vs subquery vs temp table
slides.markdown:
| | Subquery | CTE | Temp table |
|---|---|---|---|
| Readability | Nests deeply, hard to follow | Named, linear, easy to follow | Named, but needs a separate statement |
| Reused within query | No — must repeat the subquery | Yes, referenced by name multiple times | Yes |
| Materialization | Never on its own | Engine-dependent (see next slide) | Always — written to disk/temp storage |
| Scope | One query | One query (unless recursive) | Session or transaction |
| Indexable | No | No | Yes — you can add indexes to it |

**How to decide:** CTE for readability and one-query reuse; temp table when you need to index the intermediate result or reuse it across multiple statements; plain subquery only for a genuinely one-off, simple filter.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: CTE materialization is engine-dependent
slides.markdown:
A junior answer treats CTEs as "just named subqueries, always inlined the same way." A senior answer knows this varies by engine and version. Historically, **PostgreSQL before v12** always **materialized** a non-recursive CTE — ran it once, wrote the result to a temporary buffer, and could not push filters from the outer query down into it, sometimes causing surprisingly bad plans. **Postgres 12+** inlines CTEs like subqueries by default (unless marked `MATERIALIZED` or the CTE is referenced multiple times or is recursive). Other engines (SQL Server, MySQL 8+) have their own inlining rules.

The practical takeaway: if a CTE-based query is unexpectedly slow, check whether the engine materialized it — `EXPLAIN` shows a `CTE Scan` node when it did — and consider rewriting as a subquery or adding `MATERIALIZED`/`NOT MATERIALIZED` hints where supported.

A common design question: should hierarchy traversal happen in SQL (a recursive CTE) or in application code (loop, fetch children, repeat)?

A recursive CTE does the traversal in one round trip and lets the database's own indexes drive each step — far fewer network round trips for a deep or wide tree. An application-side loop is easier to debug and cap (you can bail out after N iterations trivially, log each step, add business logic mid-traversal) but pays a network round trip per level and can turn into an N+1 query pattern on a wide tree.

Interview signal: recognizing that recursive CTEs win on round trips but recursive application code wins on debuggability and flexibility is the trade-off a staff engineer names unprompted.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: forgetting a depth cap on unbounded hierarchies
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "My data doesn't have cycles, so an unbounded recursive CTE is safe."

**Why it's wrong:** cycle-free doesn't mean shallow. A category tree that's supposed to be 4 levels deep can, after years of one team nesting categories inside categories, reach 40 levels on one bad branch — and a recursive CTE with no depth cap will happily walk all 40, returning far more rows than any caller expects, or timing out on a pathological branch.

**Correct model:** add an explicit depth limit in the recursive member (`WHERE depth < 20`) even when you believe the data is well-formed. It's cheap insurance against a future data-entry mistake turning a fast query into an outage, and it documents the assumption for the next person reading the query.
